And he also taught us that we are no better than anybody, but nor are we any worse than anybody. So it's like I just always had that in my mind and I cannot think of a time with one exception that I felt intimidated or shy around any man or felt less than any man. I just like, and again, I feel so lucky and I would say if there's something I could bestow and wish upon any younger person, it would be self-confidence. I don't think we had self confidence in the sense that we were, you know, thought we were, you know, great or anything like that. But we just thought we were no better than anybody, nor any worse than anybody. And by the way, my one exception, I'll just share that with you real quick, where I was time-tied. I met John F. Kennedy, Jr. when I was an intern in Washington, D.C. And it was more just, I would have been, gosh, 20 years old. And it was more that, and he was my contemporary with the same age. And it was more like, oh my God, this guy's gorgeous. And it was just like, that's the only time I can think of like, I didn't know what to say. But other than that, I just, I feel like I've got a healthy level of self-confidence. And I've also got, to your earlier point, I have a healthy level of ambition. speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Well, I actually did not plan to run for office. I've been around politics my whole life. So my dad, his name was Gene Callahan. He passed away in 2014. But his political background was he was a journalist, wrote a five day a week political column out of Springfield, Illinois for the newspaper. At the time it was the register. Now it's the journal register. At one point went to his boss and said he needed a raise because there were he had three kids and he couldn't afford Having three kids and the editor said, well, Jane, you're already the best paid reporter in the news or I can't pay you anymore. And so he had to leave because he just like literally he and my mom couldn't afford us. And so he works for Governor Kerner back in the, so this goes way back. So the listeners will have to go the way back in their memory or they probably don't might not even have a memory, but he was a deputy press secretary. And then a guy named Sam Shapiro was the governor and he was his deputy press secretary. And then there was a guy named Paul Simon. who was running for a lieutenant governor. My dad became his chief of staff. And so, and Paul Simon hired a guy named Dick Durban, who was fresh out of law school. And so, my dad was Dick Durban's boss. And at one point, Paul Simon lived with our family. Then my dad would go on to work for a guy named Alan Dixon, who was the state treasurer, then Secretary of State and then U.S. Senator. So we have been around Democratic politicians since I was a little girl. And my grandpa was a state legislator. He was a hog farmer out of Iroquois County, which is a very Republican county, but he was a Democrat. So he was a state legislator and because we grew up in Springfield, my grandma and grandpa would stay with us when the legislature was in session. So, you know, all of this, I share all of this because these are the best, just great memories. My dad was the kind of guy who never shoot us away and would say, this is an adult conversation. You can't be here. Never did he do that. And my price of admission to sitting at the table alongside some of these legends was I would have to go to the refrigerator and pop a Budweiser forum. And I just don't remember, I'd go behind, this is probably my love of a beer to this day, but I'd duck my head down and take a quick swig and then go deliver the can of Bud to him. So I just would sit there and listen and just was fascinated by all these stories. That said, I was a political science major. but never thought I would run for office. I just, I wanted to be around people who I loved. And like these are people I loved. I just, I was fascinated by them and always, you know, we talked about being an elected official in the highest of terms. Like this was a calling, this was, these are good, honorable people. And they were always, my dad always talked about helping people. It was always through that lens. So I thought I just want to work for, for good people. So major in political science, I went to University of Maryland and got out and I interned with the Illinois State Senate. And I hated it. I mean, like I hated, I sat in a room with three other interns, two of whom I keep in touch with to this day and my friends. But we sat in this room, little bitty room, no windows and analyzed bills. all day. So we'd get these 20, 30, 40, 50 page bills and we'd have to write a one page synopsis. And I literally like, this is politics. This isn't, you know, I like to go to the events and I like to talk to people and I like to be around people and I want to help people. And so I finished that internship and it's like, I'm kind of heartbroken because I majored in this. I think this is what I want to do and I hate it. So I go back to school to the program, actually that Paul Simon founded, and you're aware of it because you went through the Public Affairs Reporting Program. But it's called Public Affairs Reporting. And now it's called University of Illinois at Springfield. And it's a journalism program. It's covering the kind of people that I knew growing up. And so I became a journalist. And by the way, a side note, I had two job offers at the end of my internship. One was at the Southern Illinois Inn here in Carbondale. And the other one was at the Quad City Times in Davenport, Iowa. So I ended up taking the Quad City Times. I always lived in the Illinois Quad Cities, though, because it's like Illinois is my home. I plan to live in Illinois the rest of my life. So I lived in Moline, Illinois, would cross the Mississippi River every day to go into work. and became a journalist. And as you know, when you're a journalist, you can't do anything politically. You cover everybody. You cover, you know, whether it's the state legislature, which I started out doing in the internship, and then covered the police beat and then City Hall, and but covered people who were running for office. So for 17 years, I was a journalist for 17 years, did not pound a yard sign. did not go to a political fundraiser, did not make a political contribution, did not knock any doors, did not do anything politically, except for a vote. And so to your question, I did not plan to run for office, and certainly I thought I'd be a journalist the rest of my life, just zero plans to ever run for office.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: I think you've got to go into everything prepared, right? And some people say that's more of a female characteristic that we can't imagine going into something high stakes and not being entirely prepared. But so in elected office, so if you want to fast forward a little bit, I'll get to the answer there. But so did that for 17 years, all of a sudden, I get a job offer out of the blue from the CEO of the local health system. I had written a profile about him. He had come from Detroit, Michigan to the Quad City. So he was newer to Illinois, had never lived in Illinois. And he realized he wanted to rebuild his entire communications team He liked the story I wrote. He liked me. He liked how I interviewed him. And so I get a call out of the blue months after I wrote that profile and they ask if I want to run their communications department. And so I initially say, no, thank you. I love what I do. And I go home that night and I tell my husband about this. And he said, why would you say no? So why would you just not listen to them? And he said, you know, you will never retire from that newspaper. Because at that point, there had been three rounds of layoffs, and you think about the state of newspapers today. But I just like, gosh, I can't imagine leaving behind this profession that I loved. I mean, I literally, I've had four professions now to this day, including if you put serving in Congress in there, I loved being a journalist more than anything else I've ever done professionally, loved it. But I ended up taking that and ended up doing that for 10 years, worked my way up to be vice president of actually a multi-billion dollar health system in multiple states. And that allowed me then to get involved in politics. All right, because I'm away from journalism. I ended up running for city council in East Malin, Illinois. This was all at the encouragement of the CEO of our health system. He wanted everybody on his senior leadership team to be involved in the community and So I ran, I was on the city council, won a competitive race there. And I love that. Like there were some days I love that more than my day job. It just was very satisfying to me. And so I'm in my 10th year of doing this and we elect in the district that I represented a Republican who identified as a tea party. who was his big issue was to get rid of the Affordable Care Act. Okay, so here I am working in healthcare. We elect this guy who's a tea partier. We elect this guy who wants to get rid of the Affordable Care Act. When I know when anybody working in healthcare knows that we were on the sense sustainable path from a cost perspective and a patient outcome perspective. And at the same time, here's another carbon-dale connection. My only brother was on his death bed. when that guy was elected and died within a week of that and had terrible medical bills because he had a long battle with cancer and luckily my mom and my dad and my sister and I and even doing fundraisers helped make sure that his family didn't have to go through bankruptcy because his bills were so terrible. So I knew we were lucky enough that we could help, but most families are not. And so that was a motivation for me. So I make a decision to run for Congress. And so I left my job in health care, ran for Congress. We can get into all kinds of side stories on that if you want to go that way. So end up defeating this guy who's an incumbent. And it's hard to defeat an incumbent member of Congress. It doesn't happen that often. But defeated him, actually beaten by six points. And in a district that, by the way, a few years later, flipped 17 points from Barack Obama in 2012 to Donald Trump in 2016. 17 points swing in the district. I ended up winning by 20 points that year that Donald Trump won the district that I represented, which was one of the biggest margins of any Democrat in the country in a Trump district. So that gets the point of your question about people who just aren't prepared, whether it's people pretending to be reporters, or whether it's people in elected office who you cannot think of any rationale why they would be either for something or get something if they actually read the bill. So yeah, there's all kinds of people who get journalism in politics that aren't prepared. Especially when you look at politics, it is, you know, you owe it to the people who elect you to do your job and to do it to the best of your ability and to be able to explain whatever your voting record is. That's part of the job. And even when you're having people yell at you and who are angry with you about a vote, you owe it to them to be able to explain. This is why I voted the way I did and to try to be rational about the explanation.

transcript: I believe that the Democratic Party has a lot of work to do in rural America. I've been a down-stater in Illinois my whole life. I've never lived in Chicago. And we had close to 10,000 family farms and 90,000 people in organized labor. So it's blue collar, it's agriculture.
